# ColorMechanism

[![CI](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/ColorMechanism/actions/workflows/main.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/ColorMechanism/actions/workflows/main.yml)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-AGPL--3.0--or--later-blue)](LICENSE)
[![CLA assistant](https://cla-assistant.io/readme/badge/sfu-cs-vision-lab/ColorMechanism)](https://cla-assistant.io/sfu-cs-vision-lab/ColorMechanism)

ColorMechanism is a MATLAB toolbox for metamer mismatch bodies and object color solids. It is the code of the paper *Metamer Mismatch Bodies: Foundations, Methods, and Applications in Color Science* [8]. The metamer mismatch body of a target holds the colors under a second mechanism of every reflectance between 0 and 1 that has the target's color under the first. The object color solid of a mechanism holds the colors of every reflectance between 0 and 1. `MetamerMismatchBody` and `ObjectColorSolid` compute them by the method you name, and every method returns the same output shape.

## Methods

| Class | Method | Bound | What it does | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MetamerMismatchBody` | `ALP` (default) | Inner | LP support in directions aimed at the gaps in its hull | [1] |
| | `Centore` | Inner | LP support on a theta-phi grid of directions | [2] |
| | `MackiewiczM1` | Inner | LP support in random directions | [3] |
| | `MackiewiczM2` | Outer | Half-spaces of the 6-D object color solid, sliced at the target | [3] |
| | `PoolAndSubset` | OuterPoints | An even spread of the vertices of several MackiewiczM2 bodies, their extremes first | [4] |
| | `ZonotopeTiling` | Exact | Tiles the 6-D zonotope, up to nchoosek(81, 6) tiles unless `AllowDenseGrid` is true | [5], [6] |
| | `Logvinenko` | Subset | Metamers with at most five transitions | [7], [8] |
| | `Stiebel` | OuterPoints | The nearest tangent plane of the 6-D object color solid along each icosphere direction, by Nelder-Mead | [9], [10] |
| | `Finlayson` | Subset | Vertices of the metamer set within a basis of reflectances, by vertex enumeration | [11] |
| `ObjectColorSolid` | `Zonotope` (default) | Exact | The zonotope of the per-wavelength vectors | [12] |
| | `Logvinenko` | Inner | Hull of a grid of two-transition spectra | [13] |
| | `Mackiewicz` | Inner | Optimal colors of random normals in orthonormal sensors | [3], [14] |

`help enums.BodyBound` defines each bound.

1. Forsythe and Funt (2026). Adaptive 3D Linear Programming for Practical Metamer Mismatch Body Computation. Extended abstract, 34th Color and Imaging Conference (CIC34), Barcelona, Spain.
2. Centore (2017). An Open-Source Algorithm for Metamer Mismatch Bodies. https://www.munsellcolorscienceforpainters.com/ColourSciencePapers/AnOpenSourceAlgorithmForMetamerMismatchBodies.pdf
3. Mackiewicz, Rivertz and Finlayson (2019). Spherical sampling methods for the calculation of metamer mismatch volumes. JOSA A 36(1), 96-104. https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSAA.36.000096
4. Forsythe and Funt (2026). Improving Uniformity of Vertex Distributions in Spherical Sampling of Metamer Mismatch Body Boundaries. Electronic Imaging 38(10), HVEI-216. https://doi.org/10.2352/EI.2026.38.10.HVEI-216
5. Forsythe and Funt (2026). What's the Right Answer Anyway? Exact Computation of Metamer Mismatch Bodies via Zonotope Tiling. Extended abstract, 34th Color and Imaging Conference (CIC34), Barcelona, Spain.
6. Forsythe and Funt (2026). Exact Discrete Metamer Mismatch Bodies from Zonotope Tiling. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22683533. Code at https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/mmb-zonotope-tiling.
7. Logvinenko, Funt and Godau (2014). Metamer Mismatching. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing 23(1), 34-43. https://doi.org/10.1109/TIP.2013.2283148
8. Forsythe and Funt (2025). Metamer Mismatch Bodies: Foundations, Methods, and Applications in Color Science. Journal of Physics: Conference Series 3128(1), 012011. 6th London Imaging Meeting (LIM 2025). https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-6596/3128/1/012011
9. Stiebel and Merhof (2018). A Robust Algorithm for Computing Boundary Points of the Metamer Mismatch Body. Color and Imaging Conference 26(1), 134-139. https://doi.org/10.2352/issn.2169-2629.2018.26.134. Code at https://github.com/tastiSaher/Metamers.
10. Stiebel and Merhof (2017). The Importance of Smoothness Constraints on Spectral Object Reflectances when Modeling Metamer Mismatching. IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops, 2985-2992. https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCVW.2017.352
11. Finlayson and Morovic (2005). Metamer sets. JOSA A 22(5), 810-819. https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSAA.22.000810
12. Centore (2013). A zonohedral approach to optimal colours. Color Research & Application 38(2), 110-119. https://doi.org/10.1002/col.20713
13. Logvinenko (2009). An object-color space. Journal of Vision 9(11), 5. https://doi.org/10.1167/9.11.5
14. Finlayson, Mackiewicz and Rivertz (2016). Computing the object colour solid using spherical sampling. Progress in Colour Studies, London, 87-88. https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/62975/
15. Forsythe and Funt (2026). Benchmarking Metamer Mismatch Body Estimates Against Exact Ground Truth. Extended abstract, 34th Color and Imaging Conference (CIC34), Barcelona, Spain.

## Requirements

- MATLAB R2023b or later
- Optimization Toolbox and Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox
- A C compiler that MATLAB supports, for the simplex MEX

## Quick Start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/ColorMechanism
cd ColorMechanism
```

Start MATLAB in that folder. Run `mex -setup C` once if MATLAB has no C compiler set up. Then open the project, build the MEX and open the tour.

```matlab
openProject("ColorMechanism.prj")
buildtool mex
open GettingStarted
```

The project puts `toolbox/`, `toolbox/doc/`, `toolbox/examples/` and `tests/` on the path.

### Note on Example Files

`toolbox/doc/GettingStarted.m` and the examples in `toolbox/examples/` are saved in the Plain Text Live Script format, introduced in MATLAB R2025a.

- In MATLAB R2025a and later, each file opens in the Live Editor with formatted text and inline output.
- In older versions, each file opens as a plain `.m` script. It runs the same, and the text shows as comments.

## Usage

```matlab
wl = (380:780)';
cmf = loadCmf("1931_2deg", wl);
d65 = loadIlluminant("D65", wl);
illA = loadIlluminant("A", wl);
cm1 = ColorMechanism(d65, cmf, wl);
cm2 = ColorMechanism(illA, cmf, wl);

mmb = MetamerMismatchBody(cm1, cm2, Reflectance=0.5);
mmb = MetamerMismatchBody(cm1, cm2, Reflectance=0.5, Method="ALP", Rounds=20, Seed=1);
mmb = MetamerMismatchBody(cm1, cm2, Reflectance=0.5, Method="Centore", FinenessIndex=5);
mmb.Volume
size(mmb.Points)
size(mmb.Vertices)
plot(mmb)

ocs = ObjectColorSolid(cm2);
ocs = ObjectColorSolid(cm2, Method="Logvinenko", GridSize=400);
metamerMismatchIndex(mmb)
```

`mmb.Points` holds the distinct points the method returned and `mmb.Vertices` the vertices of their hull, which are the rows `mmb.VertexRows` of `mmb.Points`. `mmb.Spectra` has one row per point. `nearestNeighborSpread(mmb)` measures how evenly the points are spread, those inside the hull too, as [4] does.

`compare(est, ref)` scores a body against a reference body, such as one read by `fromZonotopeTiling`, with the scores of the benchmark of [15]. `hausdorff(est, ref)` gives the exact Hausdorff distance between the two. `SupportGapPercentOfS` holds the support gaps in percent of s, the cube root of the reference's volume, as the tables of [15] give them. `SupportGapPercentOfExtent` holds them in percent of the reference's largest coordinate span.

`metamerMismatchIndex(mmb)` is the metamer mismatch index of [7], the body's volume over that of cm2's exact object color solid. It takes the body's bound, so the Centore body above gives a lower bound. Each method's options and their defaults are listed in the help of its calculator class, such as `help ALPMMBCalculator`. `mmb.Info` records the options, seed, solver and time of each run. `MetamerMismatchBody.fromZonotopeTiling(folder)` reads a case of the mmb-zonotope-tiling data [6].

`Reflectance=r` sets the target to the color of the reflectance r under cm1, where r is one value for a flat spectrum or one value per wavelength. The color is computed by the rule the method integrates with, so the target matches the method. That rule is the rectangular sum by default, the trapezoid sum with `Integration="Trapezoid"` and the trapezoid sum of `ColorMechanism`'s transition model for `Logvinenko`. A color target, `MetamerMismatchBody(cm1, cm2, XYZ)`, is used as given. `cm1.white` and `cm1.gray` are trapezoid sums, so as targets they match only the trapezoid rule.

`ColorMechanism` also computes the ADL coordinates of Logvinenko's object-color space [13], alpha, delta and lambda, with `optToAdl`. `adlToOpt` and `adlToLms` turn them back into a rectangular metamer and its color.

```matlab
rect = cm1.adlToOpt([0.5 100 550]);
adl = cm1.optToAdl(rect, cm1.wavelengths)
XYZ = cm1.adlToLms(adl)
```

## Project Structure

```
ColorMechanism/
|-- toolbox/                 library code
|   |-- doc/GettingStarted.m tour of both public classes
|   |-- examples/            further examples
|   |-- +enums/              method names, bounds and integration rules
|   `-- +pipeline/           the shared steps every method builds on, with the simplex MEX in private/
|-- tests/                   unit tests, parity tests and their data
|-- buildfile.m              clean, check, test and mex tasks
`-- ARCHITECTURE.md          design of the classes and how to add a method
```

Run `buildtool` from the root to check the code and run the tests. `CONTRIBUTING.md` lists every task.

## Citation

If you use ColorMechanism, please cite the paper and the toolbox. `CITATION.cff` holds both, with the paper as its preferred citation. If you use one of the methods, please also cite the paper in its row of the table above.

```bibtex
@article{forsythe2025metamer,
  author    = {Forsythe, Alexander and Funt, Brian},
  title     = {Metamer Mismatch Bodies: Foundations, Methods, and Applications in Color Science},
  journal   = {Journal of Physics: Conference Series},
  volume    = {3128},
  number    = {1},
  pages     = {012011},
  year      = {2025},
  publisher = {IOP Publishing},
  doi       = {10.1088/1742-6596/3128/1/012011},
  note      = {6th London Imaging Meeting (LIM 2025), London, 9--10 September 2025}
}

@software{forsythe2026colormechanism,
  author  = {Forsythe, Alexander G. and Funt, Brian},
  title   = {ColorMechanism},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/ColorMechanism}
}
```

## License

AGPL-3.0-or-later. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

The CIE tables in `toolbox/data` and the archived bodies in `toolbox/data/zonotopeTiling` and `tests/data/zonotopeTiling` are under CC BY-SA 4.0. `toolbox/data/README.md` gives the source, license and DOI of every data file.

`StiebelMMBCalculator` ports Tarek Luttermann's Metamers code, which is under the MIT license. `NOTICE` and the file's header hold that license.

The four files of Michal Mackiewicz's Metamer Mismatch Volume Toolbox in `tests/parity/mackiewicz` keep their GPL-3.0 license, whose text is in `LICENSE` in that folder. `MackiewiczM2ParityTest` runs them, and the toolbox does not.

# Individual Cone Fundamentals Toolbox (MATLAB) [![View Individual Cone Fundamentals Toolbox on File Exchange](https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/images/matlab-file-exchange.svg)](https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/184621-individual-cone-fundamentals-toolbox) [![Open in MATLAB Online](https://www.mathworks.com/images/responsive/global/open-in-matlab-online.svg)](https://matlab.mathworks.com/open/github/v1?repo=sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab) [![MATLAB Versions Tested](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/main/reports/badge/tested_with.json)](.github/workflows/main.yml) [![CI](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/actions/workflows/main.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/actions/workflows/main.yml) [![Coverage](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/main/reports/badge/coverage.json)](reports/badge/coverage.json) [![MATLAB Code Issues](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/main/reports/badge/code_issues.json)](reports/badge/code_issues.json) [![CLA assistant](https://cla-assistant.io/readme/badge/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab)](https://cla-assistant.io/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab) A MATLAB toolbox for computing **individual cone fundamentals** (observer-specific LMS spectral sensitivities and the RGB color matching functions derived from them) from biophysical parameters: opsin genotype, age, retinal field size, lens / macular / photopigment optical densities. The default Stockman & Rider (2023) photopigment + lens templates reproduce the CIE 170-1:2006 physiological standard observers (2-deg and 10-deg). Alternative templates (Govardovskii et al. 2000 for photopigments; Pokorny, Smith & Lutze 1987 and van de Kraats & van Norren 2007 for the age-dependent lens) can be substituted independently to model observer populations the CIE/S&R defaults don't cover. Output matches the reference Python implementation (`pycone`) to machine precision across the parity test suite (38 configurations × 5 output formats).


CIE 10-deg cone fundamentals (solid) vs. an age-60 observer under the van de Kraats & van Norren 2007 lens model (dashed). Each cone is peak-normalized, so age-related lens yellowing shows up as a loss of sensitivity at short wavelengths. It is visually clearest on L and M, since their peaks sit outside the lens-absorption band and are preserved by normalization, leaving the whole short-wavelength side pulled in by 30 to 40 percent. In absolute (un-normalized) units the S cone is in fact the most attenuated. Reproduced by the "Composing a figure from several observers" section of toolbox/examples/Example18_PublicationFigures.m.

## Framework The toolbox builds an L/M/S spectral sensitivity model from biophysical inputs (opsin genotype, age, retinal field size, lens and macular optical densities, per-cone photopigment optical densities, and lambda-max shifts) by traversing a four-stage pipeline: 1. **Photopigment absorbance.** A template positioned at the cone's lambda-max. 2. **Self-screening.** Beer-Lambert conversion from absorbance to relative retinal absorptance: `(1 - 10^(-OD * absorbance)) / (1 - 10^(-OD))`. 3. **Pre-receptoral filtering.** Lens and macular pigment density attenuate the retinal sensitivity to give the corneal cone fundamental. 4. **Quantal-to-energy.** Multiplication by wavelength converts photon-counting sensitivity to energy units (S&R 2023 Eq. 8). Each stage's model is swappable: photopigment template (Stockman & Rider 2023 per-cone, Stockman & Rider 2023 common, or Govardovskii 2000), lens model (Stockman & Rider 2023, Pokorny 1987, or van de Kraats & van Norren 2007), and macular template. `OutputFormat` selects which stage to return (`absorbance`, `absorptance`, `quantal`, `energy`). Defaults reproduce the CIE 170 physiological standard observers; any input can be overridden individually to model a specific observer or to study the effect of one biophysical parameter. ## Relationship to pycone [`pycone`](https://github.com/CVRL-IoO/Individual-CMFs) is the reference Python implementation of Stockman & Rider (2023). This toolbox is a MATLAB port of that model and matches pycone to machine precision on the configurations pycone supports (see [`tests/parity/README.md`](tests/parity/README.md)). It also provides some additional models for research use and a MATLAB-native interface, and a few points where the two implementations can differ in output are noted below for transparency. **Additional models** - Govardovskii et al. (2000) photopigment template (A1 and A2) for sub-400 nm extrapolation and cross-species use. - Stockman & Rider (2023) common (shape-invariant) photopigment template (Table 4 column 3): one Fourier shape translated along log-wavelength to fit any cone, for cross-species / arbitrary lambda-max use. - Pokorny, Smith & Lutze (1987) two-component age-dependent lens model. Its tabulated data start at 400 nm, and the toolbox reports nothing below that rather than flat-extrapolating. Its equations are published for ages 20-80 and the toolbox errors outside that span, because the paper does not sanction extrapolation. Table I is tabulated for a small pupil (<3 mm); scale `LensDensity` by 0.86 for a fully dilated eye (>7 mm), which the toolbox does not do for you. Prefer `VanDeKraats2007`, which is fitted from 300 nm and has an aging formula its authors state applies at any age, for sub-400 nm or out-of-span work (see the `Pokorny1987LensTemplate` class help). - van de Kraats & van Norren (2007) five-component total-ocular-media lens model with field-size-aware Rayleigh-loss coefficient and UV coverage. **Where outputs can differ from pycone** - Peak normalization: by default the toolbox locates the sub-grid peak with `fminbnd`; pycone normalizes to the discrete sample maximum. Set the normalization method to the discrete option for exact parity. - Wavelength sampling: the toolbox builds the grid with MATLAB's `(start:step:stop)'`; at fine step sizes this can differ from pycone's `np.arange` by a small floating-point amount. - Applying a lambda-max shift to the fixed Mean L template is ambiguous; the toolbox warns and uses the Serine variant. **Parameter precedence** Assigning any of `LensDensity`, `MacularDensity`, `Lod`, `Mod`, or `Sod` directly auto-engages the corresponding `Custom` density algorithm and pins that value: it is no longer recomputed when you later change `Age`, `FieldSize`, or `LensModel`. Assigning `[]` is the inverse and returns the quantity to its formula (`obs.LensDensity = []`); because one formula produces all three cone densities together, clearing any of `Lod`, `Mod`, or `Sod` reverts the group. `Custom` itself cannot be assigned to an `*Algorithm` property. It is a state that pinning a value produces. This differs from Asano, Fairchild & Blonde (2016), whose individual-observer model treats age and a separate optical-density deviation as independent parameters that compose; here a direct density assignment overrides the age / field-size formula rather than composing with it. **Ergonomics** - Round-trippable parameter snapshots via `getParameters` / `setParameters`. - Visualization: twelve plot and compare methods on `IndividualCMF` (`plotLMS`, `plotXYZ`, `plotRGBCMFs`, `plotChromaticity`, `plotAbsorbance`, `plotAbsorptance`, `plotQuantalEnergy`, `plotLens`, `plotMacular`, `plotDiagnostics`, `compareTo`, `plot`). Each draws into `gca` by default and takes `Parent=` an axes or a tile, so multi-panel figures compose with MATLAB's own `tiledlayout` / `nexttile` rather than a toolbox-specific plotter. See [`tests/parity/README.md`](tests/parity/README.md) for the configurations covered and notes on where the two implementations differ. ## Requirements - **MATLAB R2023b** or later (uses `dictionary`, `configureDictionary`, `arguments` blocks, and modern Name=Value syntax). Plain Text Live Script rendering of the examples requires R2025a or newer. - **Toolbox dependencies:** none. The toolbox uses only core MATLAB functions. ## Install The toolbox is on [MATLAB File Exchange](https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/184621-individual-cone-fundamentals-toolbox), so the quickest way to install it is from inside MATLAB. 1. In R2025a or later, open the **Add-Ons** panel from the left sidebar. In earlier releases, go to the **Home** tab and click **Add-Ons**, then **Get Add-Ons**. 2. Search for **Individual Cone Fundamentals Toolbox**. 3. Open the toolbox and install it. You can also install a release straight from GitHub. Download the latest `.mltbx` from the [GitHub Releases page](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/releases) and double-click it, or run this in the MATLAB command window to download and install the latest release. ```matlab url = "https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/releases/latest/download/individual-cmfs-matlab.mltbx"; matlab.addons.install(websave(tempname + ".mltbx", url)); ``` Either way, the toolbox adds `toolbox/` to your MATLAB path in every session and registers with the Add-On Manager, where you can uninstall it. The worked examples, the Getting Started guide and the reference documentation install with the toolbox. The test suite does not, so clone the repo if you need the tests. Once installed, the reference is in MATLAB's own Help Browser: ```matlab doc Individual Cone Fundamentals Toolbox ``` To report a problem or request a feature, open an issue at the [GitHub Issues page](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab/issues). ## Quick Start > **Tip.** Click [![Open in MATLAB Online](https://www.mathworks.com/images/responsive/global/open-in-matlab-online.svg)](https://matlab.mathworks.com/open/github/v1?repo=sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab) at the top of this README to launch the project in MATLAB Online without cloning. ```bash git clone https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/individual-cmfs-matlab.git ``` Open `individual-cmfs-matlab.prj` in MATLAB to register the project paths, then open the Getting Started guide (a one-minute orientation and a map of the examples): ```matlab edit toolbox/doc/GettingStarted.m % Click Run, or press F5 ``` ### Note on Example Files The Getting Started guide lives at `toolbox/doc/GettingStarted.m`, and the 20 worked examples live in `toolbox/examples/`. All are authored as **Plain Text Live Scripts** (R2025a or newer): they render with rich formatting in the Live Editor while remaining standard executable `.m` scripts in older MATLAB releases. Open one in the Editor for the rich-text view, or read it directly as commented code. ## Usage ```matlab % CIE 2006 10-degree standard observer (default) obs = IndividualCMF(); % CIE 2006 2-degree standard observer obs = IndividualCMF(StandardObserver=2); % StandardObserver is also a settable property: snap back to standard % after editing a custom observer obs.Age = 50; % drifts out of standard disp(obs.StandardObserver); % 0 obs.StandardObserver = 2; % snap back to 2-deg standard disp(obs.StandardObserver); % 2 % Custom observer: 60 years old, 4-degree field, van de Kraats & van Norren 2007 lens model obs = IndividualCMF(Age=60, FieldSize=4, LensModel="VanDeKraats2007"); % Genotype-driven L-cone (Alanine at codon 180) obs = IndividualCMF(Genotype=struct(L_180="Ala")); % Govardovskii (2000) continuous photopigment template obs = IndividualCMF(PhotopigmentModel="Govardovskii2000"); % Manual override engages Custom mode (preserved across Age/FieldSize edits) obs.LensDensity = 1.2; disp(obs.LensDensityAlgorithm); % "Custom" obs.LensDensity = []; % back to the model-driven value % Evaluate cone sensitivities and derived quantities. % Back to a standard observer: XYZ warns for a non-standard one, since the % transformation matrix is derived for the CIE standard. % Case follows the color-science convention: tristimulus quantities % (LMS, RGB, XYZ, V*) uppercase; chromaticity coordinates (lm, xy, ls) % lowercase. obs = IndividualCMF(); wl = (380:1:780)'; LMS = obs.LMS(wl); % L, M, S as Nx3 RGB = obs.RGB(wl); % RGB CMFs at the configured Primaries XYZ = obs.XYZ(wl); % CIE XYZ (2-deg or 10-deg matrix by FieldSize) V = obs.Luminance(wl); % V*(lambda) = y-bar row of LMS->XYZ lm = obs.lmChromaticity(wl); % LMS-sum chromaticity xy = obs.xyChromaticity(wl); % CIE xy from XYZ ls = obs.MacLeodBoynton(wl); % MacLeod-Boynton (l_MB, s_MB) % One-off query in a different output format without mutating obs A = obs.LMS(wl, OutputFormat="absorptance"); % Compare two observers obs.compareTo(IndividualCMF(Age=70), Title="Effect of aging"); % Plot methods (all accept Wavelength=, Title=, Parent= options; % plotLMS/plotAbsorbance/plotAbsorptance also accept Cones= and Log=; % plotXYZ accepts Channels=) obs.plotLMS(Cones=["L" "M"]); % L and M only, observer's OutputFormat obs.plotXYZ(Channels="Y"); % Y (luminous-efficiency) channel only obs.plotLMS(Log=true); % log10 y-axis % Multi-panel figures use MATLAB's own layout, via Parent= tiledlayout(1, 2); obs.plotLMS(Parent=nexttile()); obs.plotXYZ(Parent=nexttile()); % Build an array of observers across one parameter axis observers = IndividualCMF.across('Age', [25 50 75], ... LensModel="VanDeKraats2007", FieldSize=10); densities = [observers.LensDensity]; % Pre-receptoral filter spectra (lens + macular OD vs wavelength) lensOD = obs.getLensDensitySpectrum(wl); macularOD = obs.getMacularDensitySpectrum(wl); % Round-trip: capture, edit, restore params = obs.getParameters(); obs2 = IndividualCMF(); obs2.setParameters(params); % Export to CSV data = obs.evaluate(wl, Data="LMS"); writetable(data, "cone_fundamentals.csv"); ``` The full set of name-value options (genotype dictionary, hybrid opsin variants, per-stage algorithm choice, custom RGB primaries, normalization method, output format, log-output toggle) is documented in the `IndividualCMF` class docstring. The `toolbox/examples/` folder demonstrates each option in context. For a tour of how the toolbox is internally organized (class hierarchy, the four-stage LMS pipeline, design patterns, and how to add a new template or algorithm mode), see [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md). ## Documentation Three places, in the order most people want them: - **The Getting Started guide** is a one-minute orientation and a map of the examples. `edit toolbox/doc/GettingStarted.m`, or the Getting Started entry in the Help Browser. - **The worked examples** are twenty plain-text Live Scripts in `toolbox/examples/`, each one task, in a deliberate order. They also appear in the Help Browser with their figures, so they can be read without running anything. - **The reference**, from `doc Individual Cone Fundamentals Toolbox` after installing, covers every documented class and method. It is generated from the class help comments by `buildtool doc`, so it cannot disagree with the source, and editing a help comment is what changes the published page. The landing page opens with the tasks readers most often arrive with, each linked to the example that answers it. readme.content:
# Exact Metamer Mismatch Body Computation by Zonotope Tiling

[![MATLAB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MATLAB-R2024b--R2025b-blue.svg)](https://www.mathworks.com/products/matlab.html)
[![CI](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/mmb-zonotope-tiling/actions/workflows/main.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/mmb-zonotope-tiling/actions)
[![License: AGPL-3.0-or-later](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-AGPL--3.0--or--later-green.svg)](LICENSE)

Compute the exact metamer mismatch body (MMB), the set of colors an object
can take under a second illuminant, given its color under a first
illuminant.

The MMB is computed by tiling the six-dimensional double object-color solid
(a zonotope) into parallelotopes, slicing each tile with the target-color
plane, enumerating the cross-section vertices on a GPU and taking the
convex hull of the result. The enumeration is exact for the discretized
problem defined by the generators file. Coordinates are floating point.

The [Zenodo data archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22683533) contains
345 precomputed datasets. This repository provides the computation and
validation software, including the workflow for running new MMBs on a cluster.

## Start here

| What you want to do | Where to start | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| Explore and validate a supplied MMB | [MATLAB example](examples/GettingStarted.m) | MATLAB on a desktop or laptop, with Optimization Toolbox |
| Compute a new MMB using the supplied workflow | [Small HPC example](#small-hpc-example-start-to-finish) | A Slurm cluster with an NVIDIA GPU, CUDA and MATLAB |
| Compute the archived collection | [HPC guide](docs/HPC_GUIDE.md) | The same cluster setup |

For the MATLAB example, open `mmb-zonotope-tiling.prj`, then open and run
`examples/GettingStarted.m`. It uses the small result supplied in the
repository. No GPU or cluster connection is needed.

The functions in `src/` also prepare inputs, build hulls from existing
kernel output and validate results in MATLAB. The cluster workflow calls
these functions alongside the CUDA program that enumerates vertices on
the GPU. The job-management scripts use Slurm.

## Terminology

- The collection is the full set of MMBs defined by `runs/dataset_ids.txt`.
- A dataset is one MMB, meaning its generators file and its results.
- The `dataset_id` is the identifier of one dataset, for example
  `1931_2deg_D65_A_10nm_refl50`. It encodes the observer, the two
  illuminants, the wavelength spacing and the flat-reflectance level.

Every file a dataset owns is named after its `dataset_id`:

```
runs_output/<dataset_id>/
    generators_<dataset_id>.txt      input: the discretized problem
    chunks/                          kernel output, one file per array task
    results/
        mmb_<dataset_id>_vertices.csv
        mmb_<dataset_id>_faces.csv
        mmb_<dataset_id>_summary.txt
        mmb_<dataset_id>_gate.json   validation certificate
        .hull_verified               record written after the hull is checked
    logs/
```

## Requirements

### MATLAB on a desktop or laptop

- MATLAB for preparing inputs, loading and plotting results and building
  hulls from existing kernel output.
- Optimization Toolbox for reflectance validation, including the supplied
  MATLAB example.

These MATLAB operations do not require CUDA or Slurm. The memory needed
for hull construction depends on the size of the existing kernel output.

### HPC computation

- A Slurm cluster with at least one NVIDIA GPU. The workflow was tested on
  H100 (`sm_90`). Other architectures need `MMB_GPU_ARCH` changed in
  `config/cluster.sh`.
- CUDA toolkit with `nvcc` and a host compiler it accepts.
- MATLAB with the Optimization Toolbox. `linprog` is used for the
  reflectance feasibility check. The Parallel Computing Toolbox is optional
  and only speeds up the batch validation job.
- `bash` 4.2 or newer, `python3` 3.8 or newer, `awk` and `sha256sum` or
  `shasum`.

`python3` computes the tile count and hashes the output path for the job tag.
`awk` reads single values out of the text files.

`tools/verify_chunk.sh` and `tools/check_dataset_files.sh` need only `awk` and
`sha256sum` or `shasum`, with no MATLAB, CUDA or Slurm.

## Configure your HPC site

All site settings live in one file, `config/cluster.sh`. The launcher, the
job scripts and the environment checks read it. Edit the values, or export
the same variable names to override them.

```sh
MMB_ACCOUNT_GPU=def-funt_gpu          # Slurm account for GPU jobs
MMB_ACCOUNT_CPU=def-funt_cpu          # Slurm account for hull and validation
MMB_PARTITION=                        # empty means the cluster default
MMB_GPU_GRES=gpu:h100:1               # --gres for one GPU
MMB_EXCLUDE_NODES=                    # optional --exclude node list
MMB_MODULES_GPU="StdEnv/2023 gcc/12.3 cuda/12.2"
MMB_MODULES_MATLAB="StdEnv/2023 matlab/2024b.1"
MMB_GPU_ARCH=sm_90                    # CUDA target architecture
MMB_OUTPUT_ROOT=runs_output           # results location. Point at scratch
```

`--fmad=false` in `cuda/Makefile` is not configurable. The published
numerical results depend on it.

## Small HPC example, start to finish

This runs one 10 nm dataset through generation, enumeration, hull
construction and validation. It takes seconds of GPU time.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/mmb-zonotope-tiling.git
cd mmb-zonotope-tiling

# 1. Edit config/cluster.sh for your site, then load the toolchain.
source tools/env.sh

# 2. Build the CUDA kernel.
make -C cuda NVCC_ARCH="$MMB_GPU_ARCH"

# 3. Generate the input and submit the job.
bash mmb_run.sh runs/runs_validate_10nm.m

# 4. Watch it.
bash mmb_run.sh --status

# 5. When it reports DONE, read the summary.
cat "$MMB_OUTPUT_ROOT/1931_2deg_D65_A_10nm_refl50/results/"*_summary.txt

# 6. Validate the result against its own generators file.
matlab -batch "addpath('src'); \
  r = validateDataset('$MMB_OUTPUT_ROOT/1931_2deg_D65_A_10nm_refl50'); \
  disp(r.result)"
```

Expected values for `1931_2deg_D65_A_10nm_refl50`:

| Quantity          | Value                    |
|-------------------|--------------------------|
| Boundary vertices | 1976                     |
| Boundary faces    | 3948                     |
| Hull volume       | 1.619729587421700e+02    |
| Certificate       | PASS                     |

The volume is in the normalized coordinate frame recorded in the generators
file header (`white_y100`, perfect-diffuser Y = 100 under each illuminant).
Compare volumes only across datasets that share a normalization.

## Running the HPC workflow

`mmb_run.sh` is the entry point. It runs the requested run definition to
build generators files, then routes each dataset. Small problems go to one
GPU. Large ones are split into a job array of roughly five-minute chunks
with a dependent hull job.

```sh
bash mmb_run.sh runs/runs_survey_1931_2deg.m     # submit
bash mmb_run.sh --status                         # progress
bash mmb_run.sh runs/runs_survey_1931_2deg.m     # resume: safe to repeat
```

Re-running is the recovery path. Completed datasets are skipped, datasets
in flight are left alone and missing chunks or failed hulls are resubmitted
by index.

Job status and cancellation apply only to jobs submitted for the configured
output directory, so separate output directories can run the same dataset.
If the queue cannot be read, status and recovery stop before treating any
dataset as inactive.

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--status` | Report every dataset under the output root |
| `--dry-run` | Show routing without submitting |
| `--clean-stale` | Remove lock files for datasets with no jobs in the queue |
| `--heal` | Run `--clean-stale` and cancel jobs stuck on an unsatisfiable dependency |
| `--force-hull` | Rebuild the hull only, keeping kernel output |
| `--force-rerun` | Recompute from the kernel, keeping the generators file |
| `--force-prep` | Regenerate the generators file and recompute everything |
| `--filter PAT` | Only datasets whose id matches the regular expression PAT |
| `--chunks N` | Override the automatic chunk count |
| `--partition P` | Override `MMB_PARTITION` for this invocation |

Canceling one dataset's jobs is part of `--force-rerun` and `--force-hull`.
They cancel that dataset's queued and running jobs before recomputing.

### Choosing what to compute

`runs/*.m` are MATLAB run definitions. Each one calls `prepareGenerators`
for a set of conditions and writes generators files into the current
directory. Running one in MATLAB prepares inputs only. Passing it to
`mmb_run.sh` also submits the HPC computation.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `runs_validate_10nm.m` | The single 10 nm example above |
| `runs_1nm_d65_a.m` | The single 1 nm dataset `1931_2deg_D65_A_1nm_refl50` |
| `runs_convergence.m` | D65 paired with A, D50 and FL11 at 10, 5, 2 and 1 nm, for `1931_2deg` and `cfb_2deg` |
| `runs_survey_<observer>.m` | D65 paired with every standard illuminant, 1 nm |
| `runs_lightness_<observer>.m` | D65 paired with A, D50 and FL11 at 1 nm across reflectance levels, nine for `1931_2deg` and six for the other observers |
| `runs_observer_comparison.m` | D65 paired with A, D50 and FL11 at 1 nm and 50% reflectance, for all six observers |
| `runs_all_datasets.m` | Every dataset listed in `runs/dataset_ids.txt` |

To recompute the archived collection, use `tools/regenerate_datasets.sh`. The
procedure, including the four checks it requires first, is in
[HPC_GUIDE.md](docs/HPC_GUIDE.md).

### Writing your own run definition

```matlab
prepareGenerators("1931_2deg", "D65", ["A", "FL11"], ...
    Spacing=10, Refl=0.5, DataDir="data");
```

`help prepareGenerators` lists the options, including explicit target
tristimulus values, a reflectance spectrum instead of a flat level, custom
illuminant CSVs and batch inputs.

## How results are checked

The workflow checks input identity and file contents before accepting
kernel output. Validation then checks the resulting hull.

1. `prepareGenerators` writes the generators file and stamps the SHA-256 of
   its numeric payload into the header.
2. The CUDA kernel copies that header into its output, so every chunk
   carries the identity of the problem it solved.
3. `tools/verify_chunk.sh` checks that identity, the chunk index, the row
   count against the header, that every row is three finite
   numbers and that the completion footer is present. Only then is the
   staged file renamed to its canonical name.
4. `slurm/hull_job.sh` re-checks every chunk, requires the set to be
   complete and refuses any file belonging to another dataset. `hullMMB`
   independently repeats the provenance and completeness checks and
   re-reads its own output to confirm the volume.
5. `validateDataset` checks input identity and file consistency, recomputes
   the hull volume and looks for a bounded reflectance witness for
   sampled boundary vertices. It writes `mmb_<dataset_id>_gate.json`.
6. `validateCollection` runs `validateDataset` over `runs/dataset_ids.txt`,
   compares volumes for complementary reflectance levels and writes
   `collection_certificate.json` and `manifest_gated.txt`.

[VALIDATION.md](docs/VALIDATION.md) says what each check does and does not
cover, and [VALIDATION_FORMAT.md](docs/VALIDATION_FORMAT.md) documents the
certificate fields.

The `validation/` directory holds a comparison of the released CUDA source
with the source used for the calculation and the GPU timing of dataset_id
`1931_2deg_D65_A_1nm_refl50`. See
[`validation/README.md`](validation/README.md).

### Reading a certificate

`readValidationReport` reads a certificate and returns it as a struct. A
dataset certificate names its dataset in `dataset_id`:

```matlab
r = readValidationReport("results/mmb_1931_2deg_D65_A_10nm_refl50_gate.json");
disp(r.dataset_id)
```

## Batch validation on the HPC

To validate every dataset under the output root as a Slurm job:

```sh
. config/cluster.sh
sbatch --account="$MMB_ACCOUNT_CPU" slurm/validate_job.sh
```

Results land in `<output root>/_validation/`.

## Supported observers

| Short name | Description | Source |
|------------|-------------|--------|
| `1931_2deg` | CIE 1931 2-degree standard observer | ISO/CIE 11664-1:2019 |
| `1964_10deg` | CIE 1964 10-degree standard observer | ISO/CIE 11664-1:2019 |
| `cfb_2deg` | CIE 170-2 cone-fundamental-based 2-degree | CIE 170-2:2015 |
| `cfb_10deg` | CIE 170-2 cone-fundamental-based 10-degree | CIE 170-2:2015 |
| `lms_2deg` | LMS cone fundamentals, 2-degree | CIE 170-2:2015 Table 10.2 |
| `lms_10deg` | LMS cone fundamentals, 10-degree | CIE 170-2:2015 Table 10.5 |
| `<file>.csv` | Custom observer with four columns | Your file |

XYZ-family observers are normalized so that a perfect diffuser has Y = 100
under each illuminant. LMS observers keep the unit-peak cone fundamentals.

When the two mechanisms share a channel, the MMB is flat, and the pipeline
reports it with volume 0 and its distinct points.

### Custom observer

The observer argument also accepts a path to your own CSV, in the same way
the second illuminant does. The file has no header. Its four columns are the
wavelength in nm, then three color-matching functions or channel
sensitivities.

```
380,0.0014,0.0000,0.0065
390,0.0042,0.0001,0.0201
400,0.0143,0.0004,0.0679
```

Wavelengths must increase strictly, with no repeats, and every value must be
finite. The three channels may be negative, since color-matching functions
are signed. The file must overlap the wavelength range you ask for.

A custom observer needs `ObserverNorm`.

| `ObserverNorm` | Effect |
|----------------|--------|
| `"white_y100"` | Scale each illuminant so the second channel of a perfect reflector integrates to 100. Use this for XYZ-like color-matching functions |
| `"as_supplied"` | Use the channel values unchanged, with no white anchor |

Prepare inputs in MATLAB:

```matlab
addpath("src");
prepareGenerators("my_camera.csv", "D65", "A", ...
    Spacing=10, Refl=0.5, ObserverNorm="as_supplied", ...
    OutputDir="runs_output/my_camera_D65_A_10nm_refl50");
```

`help prepareGenerators` has the details.

## Supported illuminants

| Name | Source |
|------|--------|
| `A` | CIE standard illuminant A (ISO/CIE 11664-2:2022) |
| `D50`, `D65` | CIE daylight illuminants (ISO/CIE 11664-2:2022) |
| `E` | Equal energy, computed rather than tabulated |
| `FL1` to `FL12`, `FL3.1` to `FL3.15` | CIE fluorescent (CIE 015:2018) |
| `LED-B1` to `LED-B5`, `LED-BH1`, `LED-RGB1`, `LED-V1`, `LED-V2` | CIE LED (CIE 015:2018) |
| `<file>.csv` | Custom illuminant with two columns, wavelength in nm and relative power |

## Scale

The table gives GPU times on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, taken from the published
summaries and, for 1 nm, from
`validation/1931_2deg_D65_A_1nm_refl50/gpu_timing.md`. Datasets with the
same band count can take very different times, so the table is a rough
guide. `mmb_run.sh` routes datasets by an estimate at 0.38 billion tiles per
second. The band counts are for the CIE 1931 observer over 380 to 780 nm,
counting only complete bins. Other observers can have a shorter range.

| Spacing | Bands | Tiles, C(n,6) | One GPU | Routing |
|---------|-------|---------------|---------|---------|
| 10 nm | 40 | 3.8 million | under 1 s | single GPU |
| 5 nm | 80 | 301 million | under 1 s | single GPU |
| 2 nm | 200 | 82.4 billion | about 2 to 5 min | single GPU |
| 1 nm | 401 | 5.56 trillion | about 4 hr | chunked array |

The largest band count is 410, set by `MAX_N` in `cuda/mmb_exact_cuda.cu`.
A generators file with more bands than that is rejected rather than computed.

## Project structure

```
mmb-zonotope-tiling/
|-- config/cluster.sh          site settings, read by everything
|-- src/
|   |-- prepareGenerators.m    CIE tables -> generators_<dataset_id>.txt
|   |-- hullMMB.m              kernel output -> vertices, faces, summary
|   |-- verifyMMB.m            geometry, provenance, reflectance feasibility
|   |-- findReflectanceWitness.m
|   |-- validateDataset.m      one dataset -> certificate
|   |-- validateCollection.m   whole collection -> certificate + manifest
|   |-- readValidationReport.m reads a certificate and returns it
|   `-- compareReference.m    input and volume comparisons with the reference
|-- cuda/                      CUDA kernel and Makefile
|-- slurm/                     job scripts: single GPU, chunk array, hull, validation
|-- tools/                     environment, input copying, file checks, diagnostics
|-- runs/                      MATLAB run definitions
|   `-- dataset_ids.txt        the collection definition
|-- tests/                     MATLAB unit tests and supplied test data

|-- examples/GettingStarted.m  explore a supplied MMB in MATLAB

|-- docs/                      HPC instructions and validation reference

|-- validation/                kernel source comparison and GPU timing of one dataset
|-- .github/workflows/main.yml continuous integration, MATLAB and shell tests
```

## Testing

The MATLAB tests run in MATLAB with Optimization Toolbox. No HPC is needed.

```matlab

```

The shell tests run in a local terminal with the required shell utilities.
They simulate the cluster commands and do not submit jobs or run CUDA.


The HPC tests `tests/hpc/test_example.sh`, `tests/hpc/test_determinism.sh` and

The MATLAB unit tests use the repository's supplied test data.

The MATLAB releases and computing environments tested are recorded in

# Improving Uniformity of Vertex Distributions in Spherical Sampling of Metamer Mismatch Body Boundaries [![Open in MATLAB Online](https://www.mathworks.com/images/responsive/global/open-in-matlab-online.svg)](https://matlab.mathworks.com/open/github/v1?repo=sfu-cs-vision-lab/uniform-spherical-sampling&project=uniform-spherical-sampling.prj) ![MATLAB Versions Tested](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fsfu-cs-vision-lab%2Funiform-spherical-sampling%2Fmain%2Freports%2Fbadge%2Ftested_with.json) [![CI](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/uniform-spherical-sampling/actions/workflows/main.yml/badge.svg?cache=no)](https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/uniform-spherical-sampling/actions/workflows/main.yml) ![Coverage](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fsfu-cs-vision-lab%2Funiform-spherical-sampling%2Fmain%2Freports%2Fbadge%2Fcoverage.json) ![MATLAB Code Issues](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fsfu-cs-vision-lab%2Funiform-spherical-sampling%2Fmain%2Freports%2Fbadge%2Fcode_issues.json) [![DOI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DOI-10.xxxx%2Fxxxxx-blue)](https://doi.org/10.xxxx/xxxxx) This repository contains the MATLAB implementation for the "pool-and-subset" algorithm described in the paper *Improving Uniformity of Vertex Distributions in Spherical Sampling of Metamer Mismatch Body Boundaries*.

Standard spherical sampling methods for computing Metamer Mismatch Body (MMB) boundaries often produce non-uniform vertex distributions, with significant clustering and sparse regions. Increasing the sampling density ($N_k$) typically adds redundant vertices without resolving this non-uniformity. This project implements **Algorithm 1** from the paper, a post-processing workflow that improves uniformity while preserving geometric fidelity: 1. **Pool:** Aggregates vertices from multiple independent spherical sampling runs to create a dense candidate set ($V_{pool}$). 2. **Identify Extremes:** Identifies boundary-critical vertices (anchors) by maximizing support functions along quasi-uniform directions. These are force-included to preserve the hull geometry. 3. **Subset:** Fills the remaining vertex budget ($N_{target}$) using Seeded Farthest Point Sampling (FPS), initialized from the retained extremes. This approach substantially reduces the coefficient of variation (CV) of nearest-neighbor distances compared to baseline sampling, as shown in the figure above. ## Requirements - MATLAB R2022a or later - Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox (for `pdist2`) - Optimization Toolbox (for `linprog`) ## Quick Start > **Tip:** Click the "Open in MATLAB Online" badge above to run this project directly in your browser. This will automatically load the project and set up the path. or 1. Clone with submodules: ``` git clone --recursive https://github.com/sfu-cs-vision-lab/uniform-spherical-sampling.git ``` 2. Open the project in MATLAB: *Opening the project will automatically set up the source paths.* ```matlab openProject("uniform-spherical-sampling.prj") ``` 3. Run the getting started example: ```matlab GettingStarted ``` ### Note on Example Files The `examples/GettingStarted.m` file is saved in the **Plain Text Live Script** format (introduced in MATLAB R2025a). * **MATLAB R2025a+:** The file will open automatically in the Live Editor with formatted text, equations, and inline output. * **Older Versions:** The file will open as a standard `.m` script. It is fully executable, but the formatting (headers, descriptions) will appear as raw comments (e.g., `%[text]`). ## Usage ### 1. Pool-and-Subset (Recommended) Generate uniform vertices using the method described in the paper (Algorithm 1). ```matlab data = loadMMBTestData(); [V, info] = poolSubsetMMB(data.mech1, data.mech2, data.z0, TargetN=1000, Scale=data.yNormScale); ``` ### 2. Baseline Generation Generate baseline vertices (single spherical sampling run) as described in the paper. Requires the reference interior point (`intPoint`) for the duality transform. ```matlab data = loadMMBTestData(); V_base = generateMMBVertices(data.sensors, data.nullEqCon, data.x0, data.intPoint, NumNormals=1e5, Scale=data.yNormScale); ``` See [`examples/GettingStarted.m`](examples/GettingStarted.m) for a complete working example with visualization. ## Reproducing Paper Results The `paperFigures/` directory contains scripts to regenerate all figures and tables from the paper: ```matlab cd paperFigures generateAll % Runs all figure and table generation scripts ``` Individual scripts: * `generateFigure1.m` - Convex hull visualization * `generateFigure2.m` - Single-run vertex distribution * `generateFigure3.m` - Run-to-run variability * `generateFigure4.m` - CV comparison swarm plots * `generateFigure5.m` - Baseline vs pool+subset comparison * `generateTable1.m` - Baseline sweep results * `generateTable2.m` - Pool+subset results Outputs are saved to `paperFigures/output/`. ## Project Structure ``` uniform-spherical-sampling/ ├── src/ # Core algorithm implementation │ ├── poolSubsetMMB.m │ ├── generateMMBVertices.m │ ├── seededFPS.m │ ├── identifyExtremeVertices.m │ └── computeNNStats.m ├── paperFigures/ # Paper figure/table generation │ ├── generateFigure*.m │ ├── generateTable*.m │ ├── generateAll.m │ └── utils/ # Shared plotting utilities ├── tests/ # Unit tests ├── examples/ # Usage examples │ └── GettingStarted.m ├── buildUtilities/ # Build task helpers (badge generation) ├── reports/ # Generated test/coverage reports ├── resources/ # MATLAB Project configuration files └── lib/ # External dependencies (submodules) ``` ## Citation If you use this code in your research, please cite: ```bibtex @inproceedings{Forsythe2026, author = {Forsythe, Alexander G. and Funt, Brian}, title = {Improving Uniformity of Vertex Distributions in Spherical Sampling of Metamer Mismatch Body Boundaries}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the IS\&T Electronic Imaging Symposium (EI 2026)}, year = {2026}, note = {In Press} } ``` This algorithm makes use of the algorithm described in ```bibtex @article{mackiewicz2018spherical, title={Spherical sampling methods for the calculation of metamer mismatch volumes}, author={Mackiewicz, Michal and Rivertz, Hans Jakob and Finlayson, Graham}, journal={Journal of the Optical Society of America A}, volume={36}, number={1}, pages={96--104}, year={2018}, publisher={Optical Society of America} } ``` ## License This code is provided under the AGPL v3 License terms specified in the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file Copyright 2026 Alexander Forsythe and Brian Funt, Simon Fraser University.

# Adelson's Checkerboard Shadow Illusion

A GLSL recreation of Adelson's checker shadow illusion. A light tile in shadow and a dark tile in direct light appear different, but have the same display code value.

Paste `checkerboard.glsl` into a new shader on [Shadertoy](https://www.shadertoy.com) to run it.

## Description

This shader raymarches a cylinder casting a soft shadow on a checkerboard. Parameters are tuned so a selected dark square in direct light and a selected light square in shadow render to similar linear intensities, recreating Adelson’s checker-shadow lightness illusion.

## Reference

* **Adelson, E. H. (2000).** Lightness Perception and Lightness Illusions. In M. Gazzaniga (Ed.), *The New Cognitive Neurosciences* (2nd ed., pp. 339–351). Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
* **Adelson, E. H. (1995).** Checkershadow Illusion. [Perceptual Science Group, MIT](https://persci.mit.edu/gallery/checkershadow).

# CMMRI: Color Sensor Accuracy Index

A MATLAB implementation of the **Camera Metamer Mismatch Radii Index (CMMRI)**. This metric evaluates the colorimetric accuracy of digital cameras by calculating the Metamer Mismatch Body (MMB) induced by the camera sensors relative to the human standard observer.

## Reference
```bibtex
@article{Roshan2020,
    author = {Roshan, Emitis and Funt, Brian},
    title = {Color Sensor Accuracy Index Utilizing Metamer Mismatch Radii},
    journal = {Sensors},
    volume = {20},
    number = {15},
    year = {2020},
    article-number = {4275},
    url = {https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/20/15/4275},
    doi = {10.3390/s20154275}
}

```

## Usage

The main entry point for the algorithm is `CMMRI.m`.

1. Ensure the data files `Canon500D.mat` and `D65_6500k.xlsx` are in your MATLAB path.
2. Run the script:

```matlab
CMMRI
```

The script calculates the Metamer Mismatch Volume (MMV) for a mid-grey sample and outputs the average MMV dimension.

## Key Files

* **`CMMRI.m`**: The main execution script.
* **`Canon500D.mat`**: Sample camera sensor sensitivities.
* **`D65_6500k.xlsx`**: Standard D65 illuminant data.
* **`calculate_mmv.m`**: Optimization routine for finding metameric boundaries.

## Requirements

* **MATLAB** (R2020a or later recommended)
* **Optimization Toolbox**

# Thin-Plate Spline Illumination Estimation Automatic White Balancing Method

[![Open in MATLAB Online](https://www.mathworks.com/images/responsive/global/open-in-matlab-online.svg)](https://matlab.mathworks.com/open/github/v1?repo=sfu-cs-vision-lab/tps)

### Abstract
Thin-plate spline interpolation is used to interpolate the chromaticity of the color of the incident scene illumination across a training set of images. Given the image of a scene under unknown illumination, the chromaticity of the scene illumination can be found from the interpolated function. The resulting illumination-estimation method can be used to provide color constancy under changing illumination conditions and automatic white balancing for digital cameras. A thin-plate spline interpolates over a nonuniformly sampled input space, which in this case is a training set of image thumbnails and associated illumination chromaticities. To reduce the size of the training set, incremental k medians are applied. Tests on real images demonstrate that the thin-plate spline method can estimate the color of the incident illumination quite accurately, and the proposed training set pruning significantly decreases the computation.

# Rectangular and Wraparound Gaussian colour coordinates

For more information see: [Metamer Mismatching](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIP.2013.2283148)

### Abstract

A new algorithm for calculating the metamer mismatch volumes that arise in colour vision and colour imaging is introduced. Unlike previous methods, the proposed method places no restrictions on the set of possible object reflectance spectra. As a result of such restrictions, previous methods have only been able to provide approximate solutions to the mismatch volume. The proposed new method is the first to characterize precisely the metamer mismatch volume for any possible reflectance.

### Citation

```
@article{6606818,
  author={Logvinenko, Alexander D. and Funt, Brian and Godau, Christoph},
  journal={IEEE Transactions on Image Processing}, 
  title={Metamer Mismatching}, 
  year={2014},
  volume={23},
  number={1},
  pages={34-43},
  keywords={Color;Image color analysis;Sensors;Solids;Equations;Sensitivity;Vectors;Colour vision;metamerism;metamer mismatching;metamer set;metamer mismatch volume},
  doi={10.1109/TIP.2013.2283148}}
```

also see: [The Extent of Metamer Mismatching](https://summit.sfu.ca/item/18189)

### Abstract

Metamer mismatching refers to the fact that two objects reflecting light causing identical colour signals (i.e., cone response or XYZ) under one illunimation may reflect light causing non-identical colour signals under a second illumination_ As a consequence of metamer mismatching, two objects appearing the same under one illuminant can be expected to appear different under the second illunimant. To investigate the potential extent of metamer mismatching, we calculated the metamer mismatching effect for 20 Munsell papers and 8 pairs of illunimants (Logvinenko & Tokunaga, 20 11) using the recent method (Logvinenko, Funt, & Godau, 2012) of computing the exact metan2er mismatch volume boundary. The results show that metamer mismatching is very significant for some lights. In fact, metamer mismatching was found to be so significant that it can lead to the prediction of some paradoxical phenomena, such as the possibility of 20 objects having the same colour under a neutral ("white") light dispersing into a whole hue circle of colours under a red light, and vice versa.

### Citation

```
  booktitle={Proc. AIC 2013 International Colour Association Conference},
  volume={2},

}
```
